722.title: Beautiful patience
722.hook: losing Joseph, Jacob says: patience is most fitting, a beautiful patience
722.carry: his eyes go white with grief
722.howItsDone: Some Muslims say sabrun jamil, beautiful patience, to one another in long trials, and the story of Jacob and Joseph in the twelfth surah is told as a lesson in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Umm Salama, the widow who said: to God we return. Your line was who could be better than him.

Evening. A group of brothers comes home crying, carrying their little brother's shirt. There's blood on it. A wolf took him, they say, while we were racing and left him with our things. Their father, Jacob, holds the shirt. In the Quran's telling, he doesn't believe them. The blood is false, and somehow he knows it. His favorite son is gone, the ones in front of him are lying, and he has to answer right there, in that room. The twelfth chapter of the Quran, the chapter of Joseph, gives his answer in two Arabic words.
screen: `BROTHERS COME HOME CRYING.` → `A SHIRT WITH FALSE BLOOD.` → `JACOB HAS TO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Jacob tells his sons that their own souls have talked them into something. And then: sabrun jamil. Patience, beautiful. Not grim patience, not gritted teeth. And he adds: it is God whose help is sought against what you describe. He doesn't shout, and he doesn't pretend to believe them. Second, what it isn't. Beautiful patience is not dry-eyed. Later in the chapter, when another son is lost, Jacob says the same two words again. Then he turns away and says, alas for Joseph, and his eyes go white with grief. In the Quran, a patient man's grief is plain to see. Third, where the complaint goes. When his sons tell him to stop dwelling on Joseph, Jacob answers that he complains of his grief and sorrow only to God, and knows from God what they don't. Some commentators describe beautiful patience in just these terms: grief carried to God, without bitterness poured out on the people around you. He sends his sons to search for Joseph, and tells them not to despair of God's mercy. Fourth, the shape of it. Sabr, from two days ago, met the first blow. Beautiful patience is the long version: a long separation, with grief, honesty and hope, and without turning the hurt into a weapon. The story, in the end, gives Joseph back. But Jacob chose his patience long before he knew that.
screen: `SABRUN JAMIL: PATIENCE, BEAUTIFUL.` · `IT GRIEVES.` · `THE COMPLAINT GOES TO GOD.` · `A LONG PATIENCE, WITHOUT BITTERNESS.` · then, large: `BEAUTIFUL PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Find one situation you're having to be patient with, a person who hurt you, a wait that won't end, and notice whether the patience has an edge: a sigh, a story you keep telling about who's to blame. Let the hurt be fully there, and let the edge soften on each out-breath. If you pray, you can bring the complaint to God the way Jacob did; if not, simply set it down, out of reach of anyone you might aim it at.
Beautiful patience: sabrun jamil, Jacob's words in the Quran on losing Joseph. Patience that grieves, and takes its complaint to God. Today's word.
Your line: his eyes go white with grief. In this story, patience still weeps. Until tomorrow.

723.title: Ayyub called out
723.hook: the Quran's Job, patient in affliction, calls to God and is answered
723.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Ayyub's words from Quran 21:83 as a supplication in illness and hardship, and his story is told as an example of patience that still turns to God for help.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was beautiful patience, Jacob's grief carried to God. Your line was his eyes go white with grief.

Some people will carry a heavy box up the stairs, arms shaking, rather than ask the neighbor on the landing to grab one end. For them, asking can look like failing, as if patience means silence, and silence means strength. Not long ago, this path met Job in the Bible: the good man who lost everything and argued with God. The Quran knows him too, and calls him Ayyub. And the Quran, which praises his patience, also remembers the moment he opened his mouth and asked.
screen: `CARRYING THE BOX ALONE.` → `JOB HAS A NAME IN THE QURAN.` → `AYYUB OPENS HIS MOUTH.`

segments.voice: First, who he is. The Quran tells Ayyub's story in short passages. It doesn't stage long debates with friends. It gives his affliction, his prayer, and the answer. Second, the call. In the chapter of the Prophets, Ayyub cries out to his Lord: harm has touched me, and you are the most merciful of those who show mercy. That's all. He doesn't demand a reason, and he doesn't hide the pain. He says two true things side by side: this hurts, and you are merciful. Third, the answer. The very next verse says God answered him, removed the harm, and gave him back his family and as many again with them, a mercy, and a reminder for those who worship. In another chapter, the answer is physical: strike the ground with your foot, and there is cool water, to wash in and to drink. Fourth, the surprise. In that same passage, after the call and the healing, God says: We found him patient. How excellent a servant. The man who called out is the one the Quran calls patient. In this telling, asking isn't the opposite of patience. Sabr holds steady; it doesn't mean pretending to be fine. The Bible's Job argues; the Quran's Ayyub calls. Each book remembers him its own way, and neither has him stay silent.

724.title: Arjuna drops his bow
724.hook: on the battlefield, Arjuna sinks down in despair
724.howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita is read and recited at home, in temples and in study groups, and its first chapter, Arjuna's despair, is heard as the opening that makes the teaching possible.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ayyub, the Quran's Job, who named his harm and was still called patient. Your line was he called out.

Conch shells blow. Two armies face each other on a wide field called Kurukshetra. A chariot rolls out between them, carrying the archer Arjuna, with his friend Krishna holding the reins. Arjuna asked for this: drive me out, let me see who I'm fighting. And he looks across the field and sees the faces. Not strangers. His teachers. Grandfathers. Cousins, uncles, friends. The Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture set inside the epic Mahabharata, begins right here, with a hero falling apart.
screen: `TWO ARMIES, READY.` → `DRIVE ME OUT. LET ME SEE.` → `HE SEES THE FACES.`

segments.voice: First, the body. The Gita doesn't make Arjuna's despair noble or tidy. It makes it physical. His limbs give way, he says, his mouth goes dry, his body trembles, his hair stands on end. His great bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand, and his skin burns. He can't stand; his mind is reeling. Second, the reasons. What good is a kingdom won by killing the people I love? I don't want victory, or pleasures, or a throne, if this is the price. His argument is serious, and the text lets him make all of it. Third, the drop. At the end of the first chapter, Arjuna casts away his bow and arrows and sinks onto the chariot seat, his mind overwhelmed with grief. At the start of the second, he tells Krishna plainly, I will not fight, and falls silent. Tradition names the whole first chapter for his despair. Fourth, why it matters. All of Krishna's teaching comes after this collapse, and in answer to it. Tradition says Krishna here is God, teaching his friend; some readers also hear the battle as the struggle inside any person. Either way, the conversation doesn't begin while Arjuna is pretending to be fine. It begins when he puts the bow down and admits he doesn't know what to do. The text opens its wisdom to a person in despair, not to one who has it together.
screen: `HIS LIMBS GIVE WAY.` · `WHAT GOOD IS A KINGDOM?` · `HE CASTS AWAY THE BOW.` · `THE TEACHING BEGINS AFTER.` · then, large: `I WILL NOT FIGHT.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle into the seat, the way Arjuna sank onto his, and admit silently one despair, one thing you don't know how to face. Say it plainly to yourself, I don't know what to do about this, and feel what the body does: maybe a tightening, maybe a little release. You don't need an answer yet; Arjuna didn't have one either.
Gandiva, Arjuna's bow in the Gita, slips from his hand as despair overtakes him before Krishna's teaching begins. Today's word.
Your line: dropped the bow. Krishna's teaching began there, with the bow down, not before. See you tomorrow.

725.title: Heat and cold
725.hook: Krishna: pleasure and pain come and go like heat and cold; bear them
725.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers point to Gita 2.14 when teaching steadiness in pleasure and pain, and some practices of fasting, austerity and meditation are understood as training in this endurance, titiksha.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Gandiva, Arjuna's bow, cast aside in despair. Your line was dropped the bow.

Step out of a warm house into a winter morning and the cold hits like a slap. A little way into the walk, you've half forgotten it. A summer afternoon's heat presses down; by evening a breeze comes and it's gone. Nobody takes the weather personally for long. It arrives, it stays a while, it leaves. In the Gita, Arjuna has just said I will not fight and fallen silent. The text says Krishna answers him, as if smiling. And early in that answer, he reaches for the weather.
screen: `THE COLD HITS LIKE A SLAP.` → `BY EVENING, THE HEAT IS GONE.` → `KRISHNA ANSWERS, AS IF SMILING.`

segments.voice: First, the contacts. In the second chapter of the Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that the touch of the senses on the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. The Sanskrit calls these matra-sparsha, the contacts of the senses. Second, what they do. They come and go, Krishna says. They don't last. The verse takes things we'd usually sort into good and bad, pleasure and pain, and gives them the same nature: arriving, and leaving. Third, the instruction. Bear them, Arjuna. The Sanskrit word is titikshasva: bear it, put up with it. Not enjoy it, not deny it. Stay standing while it passes through. The next verse names the reward: the steady person whom these don't throw off balance, the same in pain and pleasure, is fit, Krishna says, for what doesn't die. Fourth, what it isn't. This isn't a teaching that pain is unreal, or that Arjuna's grief is foolish. Krishna is speaking to a man slumped on a chariot seat, and he starts small, with a picture: feelings, even huge ones, are like weather. Hindu teachers read this verse in different ways, some as a first step toward knowing the self, some as training for steady action. Each reading starts from the same line. What arrives can be borne, partly because it will also leave.

segments.voice: Notice one small discomfort already present, an itch, a stiff shoulder, cool air on your hands, and don't fix it; bear it, the way Krishna asks. Watch it closely: does it stay exactly the same, or shift, rise, fade, come back? You're not fighting it and not giving in to it, just staying standing while it passes through.
Titikshasva, Krishna's Sanskrit word in the Gita for bearing heat and cold, pleasure and pain, without being thrown off balance. Today's word.

726.title: The uncut self
726.hook: weapons can't cut the self, fire can't burn it
726.howItsDone: These verses of the Gita's second chapter are recited, and some families read them at funerals and memorials as a teaching about the self that does not die.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was titikshasva: bear the heat and cold, pleasure and pain. Your line was they come and go.

An old photograph: a small child on a beach, squinting into the sun. Nearly everything has changed since: the face, the voice, the opinions, the fears. And yet the grown-up holding the photo points at the child and says: that's me. What is the me that carries across? Arjuna's grief on the chariot is about bodies: the people he loves will die. Krishna's answer, early in the second chapter of the Gita, turns to something he says no blade can reach.
screen: `A CHILD ON A BEACH.` → `EVERYTHING HAS CHANGED.` → `AND YET: THAT'S ME.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self, the one who lives in the body, is never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is killed. Second, the old clothes. As a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, Krishna says, so the embodied self leaves worn-out bodies and takes up new ones. The body changes the way clothes do; the wearer goes on. Third, four forces. Weapons do not cut it. Fire does not burn it. Water does not wet it. Wind does not dry it. Four things that can wreck a body, and none of them reaches it. The next verse gives today's word: acchedya. Uncuttable. Steady, unmoving, ancient, the text says. Fourth, how Hindus hold it. The self here is the atman, and Hindu schools understand it differently. Some teach that the self, at its depth, is one with the ultimate reality, Brahman. Others teach that each self is eternal and distinct, and belongs to God in love. They share this verse. And the setting is hard to forget: Krishna says this on a battlefield, to a man about to fight his own family, and some readers wrestle with that. Others, in their suffering, find in the verse a place to stand. The pain is real, and it comes and goes. Beneath it, Krishna says, is what was never cut.

segments.voice: Watch what's changing, the breath rising and falling, a sound in the room, a thought passing, and let each one come and go. Then gently turn toward whatever is noticing all of it: the sounds change, but does the hearing? If something feels steady while everything else moves, rest there, without trying to name it or grab it.

727.title: Sweet is your will
727.hook: a line about sweetness that Sikh tradition ties to Guru Arjan's death in Lahore, and to accepting God's will (Guru Granth Sahib 394)
727.howItsDone: Sikhs sing tera kiya meetha laagai in kirtan, and they remember Guru Arjan's martyrdom with gatherings and with chhabeel, stalls that offer cool sweetened water to anyone passing by.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was acchedya, the uncut self no weapon reaches. Your line was uncut.

Tera kiya meetha laagai. Sikhs sing this line, and it means, roughly: what you do tastes sweet to me. On paper it sounds like a line for a good day: a wedding, a new baby, a harvest in. But Sikh memory ties it to Guru Arjan, one of the Sikh Gurus, and to the end of his life. Tradition says he was arrested and held in Lahore, tortured there, and died, and that this was the line he lived inside while it happened.
screen: `TERA KIYA MEETHA LAAGAI.` → `A LINE FOR A GOOD DAY?` → `SIKH MEMORY TIES IT TO LAHORE.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. It sits on page 394 of the Guru Granth Sahib, in a hymn by Guru Arjan, and runs, in paraphrase: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Name. Nanak there is a signature: the later Gurus sign their hymns with the first Guru's name. It doesn't say what you do is easy, or fair, or what I'd have chosen. Meetha is a taste word, sweet in the mouth. And the hymn asks for one thing back: not a way out, the Name. Second, the story. Sikh tradition tells that the Guru was made to sit on a hot iron plate while burning sand was poured over him. The accounts differ in their details, and historians weigh them. What tradition holds onto most is not the cruelty but his calm. Third, the friend. Tradition says the Sufi saint Mian Mir, a Muslim and a friend of the Guru, offered to step in and plead for him, and the Guru asked him not to. This too, he said, is the will. Sikhs call that will bhana, what pleases God, and remember Guru Arjan as a picture of accepting it. Fourth, what it isn't. Accepting the will is not folding your hands or calling evil good. The same tradition remembers his death as a wrong done to him, and honors him as a martyr. And it holds acceptance right beside chardi kala, rising spirits, which this path met in its first year. Acceptance here isn't defeat. It's refusing to let the pain decide who you are.
screen: `A TASTE WORD: MEETHA, SWEET.` · `THE HOT PLATE AND THE CALM.` · `A FRIEND OFFERS TO STEP IN.` · `NOT DEFEAT: RISING SPIRITS.` · then, large: `SWEET IS YOUR WILL.`

segments.voice: Hold one thing you can't change, small enough for two minutes: a delay, a diagnosis, a choice someone else already made. Breathe in and say inside, this is what is; breathe out and let one place that's pushing against it, the jaw, the shoulders, the stomach, stop pushing for a breath or two. Nobody asks you to call it sweet; if you pray, hold the Guru's line, tera kiya meetha laagai, or simply, this is what is.
Bhana, the Sikh word for what pleases God, accepting what can't be changed without going bitter and without giving up. Today's word.
Your line: this too is the will. Here, acceptance sits right beside rising spirits. Until tomorrow.

728.title: Within the order
728.hook: Sikhs speak of hukam, the divine order, to live within rather than fight (Japji 1–2)
728.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Japji as part of their morning prayers, and they speak of living in the hukam, or in God's bhana, when they meet what they can't change.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bhana, the will, and Guru Arjan's line: sweet is your will. Your line was this too is the will.

Two people get caught in the same downpour. One stands under an awning, glaring at the sky, phone out, typing how unfair this is. The other pulls up a hood and walks, and halfway home notices the gutters running like small rivers. Same rain. Same wet socks. Something different in how they stand inside it. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with a long poem by Guru Nanak called the Japji, part of the Sikh morning prayers. Near its start, Nanak asks a question, and answers it with one word.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE, ONE DOWNPOUR.` → `THE JAPJI ASKS A QUESTION.` → `THE ANSWER IS ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the question. In the first stanza of the Japji, Nanak asks, in paraphrase: how can we become true, and how does the wall of falsehood come down? He's already set aside the easy answers. Thinking it over won't do it. Keeping silent won't do it. Piling up what you want won't satisfy the hunger. Then the answer: walk in the hukam, the order of the will, which is written along with you. Second, the word. Hukam means an order, a command. But in the Japji it isn't a boss shouting instructions. It's the order everything is already moving inside. The second stanza spells it out: by the hukam bodies take shape; by the hukam some are high and some low; by the hukam pain and pleasure come. Then: everyone is within the hukam; no one is outside it. Third, who argues. The stanza ends, in paraphrase: Nanak, whoever understands the hukam doesn't speak in haumai, in ego. That's the turn. The pain is inside the order. What fights the order is the self that says this shouldn't be happening to me. Fourth, what it isn't. Living within the hukam isn't lying down in the road. Sikhs work, serve, and stand up for others, and they do it inside the order too. The rain doesn't change. The quarrel with it does.
screen: `HOW DOES THE WALL OF FALSEHOOD FALL?` · `HUKAM: THE ORDER EVERYTHING MOVES IN.` · `EGO IS WHAT ARGUES.` · `NOT LYING DOWN IN THE ROAD.` · then, large: `NO ONE IS OUTSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Notice what's already happening without your permission, the breath, your heartbeat if you can find it, a sound outside, the air on your hands, and let each be there: this, too, is happening. Then call up one thing today you've been fighting, a slow line, a printer that won't print, and picture yourself walking through it with the hood up instead of standing under the awning.
Hukam: Punjabi, an order or command. In the Japji, the divine order everything moves within; no one is outside it. Today's word.

Your line: no one is outside it. The week ran from Jacob's beautiful patience, Ayyub calling out, Arjuna's dropped bow, titikshasva, acchedya and a Guru's sweet will to the hukam. That's day seven hundred twenty-eight, and a week.
